entries.previousTitle: Planning Fallacy – when you think things will take less time than they do
entries.title: Planning Fallacy – when plans make completion times look too optimistic
entries.description:
Planning Fallacy is the tendency to predict that your own task or project will finish sooner than it actually does, even when similar work has taken longer before.

🔍 Where can it show up?
- Project estimates – a team builds a detailed plan for smooth execution but gives too little weight to delays in comparable past projects.
- Personal tasks – you picture how writing, studying, moving, or renovating will go if the main steps work as planned, while interruptions and rework receive less attention.
- Delivery reviews – a late project is explained as an unusual case, so the next estimate starts from another fresh plan instead of learning from the history.

💡 A better check
- Start with comparable past work: how long did similar tasks actually take?
- Give a range and name the main sources of uncertainty instead of promising one precise date.
- Keep the original estimate and assumptions so you can compare them with the eventual result.
- Do not use a universal buffer such as ‘multiply by 1.5’. The useful adjustment depends on the task, the data and the reference class.
entries.reason: The legacy page correctly described optimistic time estimates but recommended a universal 1.5 multiplier. The reviewed literature supports using relevant past experience and outside-view information, not one fixed correction for every task.
